message_content: Can you walk me through what you want this interactive television messaging demo to achieve in your business context, and how you would know it has been successful?

We want it to show that an interactive TV can be more than just passive viewing and can support a familiar messaging experience on the screen. In business terms, the demo should prove that users can log in, see friends, chat, manage their status, and understand what others are watching, without making the TV experience feel awkward or too complex.
We would see it as successful if people can use it easily on a television interface and immediately understand the value of the platform. It would also be a good sign if the demo reliably shows presence, messages, and notifications, because that would demonstrate the communication capability we want to highlight.
Who is the primary audience you want this demo to impress, and what specific viewing or messaging scenario should they see on the television to best understand the platform’s value?

The primary audience is really our internal business and technical stakeholders, along with potential partners who need to see what the platform can do. We want them to see a simple, believable living-room scenario where a user signs in, sees a few friends online, notices what they are watching, and sends a message from the TV while watching something themselves. That should make the value obvious because it shows communication happening in the same context as television viewing rather than on a separate device.
Given that living-room scenario, what devices or television environments do you need the platform to work on, and are there any important limits on where or how it should be expected to run?

We want it to work on the interactive television platform itself, so the key environment is a TV set-top or similar platform where the user is already watching content and using a remote or simple on-screen controls. I don’t think we’re trying to support every kind of TV hardware or a fully general home computer setup for this demo, just the intended Philips platform environment. If there are specific decoding or interface limits, I’d need to check with the technical team, but the expectation is that it runs reliably in that TV context.
What business or user information do you need to protect when people send messages or appear online in this TV experience, and how would you want that information to be used or shared?

We need to protect the user’s account identity, their buddy list, and the content of their messages, since those are personal. Presence information should be limited to what the user has chosen to show, like online status and what program they’re watching, because that’s part of the experience but still needs to be handled carefully. I’d expect that information to be visible only to contacts the user allows, and definitely not exposed broadly outside the messaging service.
Are there any specific rules for how long chat content should be kept, or situations where messages need to be deleted sooner or retained longer?

For the demo, I don’t think we have a formal retention policy defined yet. My assumption is that messages should stay available at least during the active session so users can see the conversation, but beyond that we’d need to confirm whether anything should be stored persistently at all. If there are legal or product requirements for retention or deletion, I’d need to verify that with the team.

When the service is being used live, what kinds of interruptions or failures matter most to you, and what should happen for users in those moments so the experience can continue or recover as smoothly as possible?

The biggest concern is anything that breaks sign-in, message delivery, or the visible presence display, because that would undermine the whole demo. If there’s a temporary service or network interruption, I’d want the user to get a clear indication that the connection is unavailable and then have the system recover gracefully once service returns, rather than losing the whole session immediately. If a message can’t be sent, it should be obvious to the user so they know whether to retry.
What is the maximum delay you’d consider acceptable for messages to appear and presence status to refresh before it feels too slow for the demo?

For the demo, it needs to feel close to real time. Ideally messages and presence updates should appear within a few seconds, and anything noticeably longer than that would start to feel slow to viewers. I don’t have an exact hard number yet, but I’d want it tight enough that the interaction still feels immediate on the TV.
What should the on-screen chat experience feel like for viewers using the TV, and how would you want them to move through messages, contacts, and any other parts of the conversation flow?

It should feel very simple and readable from a distance, since people will be using it from the couch. The flow should let them move easily between their buddy list, the current conversation, and sending a reply without a lot of steps or clutter. I’d want the screen to stay focused on the active chat and presence information, with navigation that feels straightforward and not like a typical desktop messenger.

When you talk about presence and nicknames for this experience, what do those labels need to communicate to viewers, and how should you want them to be used in the app when people are browsing the buddy list or opening a chat?

The nickname should identify the person in a friendly, recognizable way, since that’s what people will see first on TV. Presence needs to clearly show whether someone is online and, if available, what they’re watching, so viewers immediately understand who is available and what’s happening. In the buddy list and chat view, those labels should be shown consistently and updated as soon as they change.
What presence states should television users be able to choose from beyond simply online and watching, if any?

At minimum, I’d expect online, busy, and away, because those are the most useful statuses for letting people know whether to contact someone. I’m not sure we need a large set of custom states for the first version, since the experience should stay simple on TV. If the team wants more later, we could look at that, but I’d keep it basic for now.

When a user is signed in but the app can’t reach the service briefly, what should they be able to keep doing in the buddy list and presence display, and what should change on screen until the connection comes back?

If the connection drops briefly, I’d still want the user to be able to look at their existing buddy list and whatever was already on screen, so the app doesn’t feel like it has completely frozen. What should change is the freshness of the data: the presence indicators should make it clear that updates may be delayed, and sending or receiving new messages should be shown as unavailable until the connection returns. Once it comes back, I’d expect the app to refresh automatically without making the user start over.

When the buddy list is displayed, are there any rules for how contacts should be ordered or grouped—for example by availability, recent activity, or favorites—or should it always stay in one fixed order?

I’d prefer the list not be completely fixed if we can avoid it. The most useful behavior would be to surface people who are online or active near the top, since that’s what matters most for quick TV interactions, while still keeping a stable, understandable order overall. I’m not certain we need more advanced grouping like favorites in the first version, unless it comes up as necessary during testing.

How should the list behave when someone’s availability changes or they come online and go offline—should it re-sort immediately, and if so, are there any limits on how much movement is acceptable so the order still feels stable?

Yes, it should update when availability changes, but I’d want it to do that gently so the list doesn’t jump around too much. Moving someone up when they come online makes sense, but constant reshuffling would be distracting on a TV screen. So the order should stay mostly stable, with only small, meaningful changes when status changes.

How do you want blocking and unblocking to work in the experience from a user’s point of view—what should happen when someone blocks a contact, and what should change again if they later unblock them?

Blocking should be simple and very clear from the user’s perspective. If someone blocks a contact, that person should no longer be able to send them messages, and they should effectively disappear from normal conversation access in the app. If they later unblock them, the contact should become available again for messaging and appear normally in the buddy list, assuming they’re otherwise allowed to be there.
When a contact is blocked, what should happen to their incoming messages or notifications—should they be hidden, dropped, or shown in some specific blocked-state behavior?

They should be dropped from the user’s normal experience rather than shown as new messages. I wouldn’t want blocked contacts creating visible notifications or cluttering the chat view, because that defeats the purpose of blocking. If there’s any indication at all, it should be something subtle in the settings or contact management area, not in the main messaging flow.

Should any of a user’s identity, buddy list, message content, or presence details ever be visible outside the contacts they’ve explicitly allowed, and if so, what specific situations or exceptions should govern that visibility?

In general, no, those details should stay within the user’s allowed contacts and not be broadly visible. The one exception I’d expect is the minimal presence signal needed for the service to work, like showing that someone is online to their buddies and what program they’re watching if that’s part of the social experience. Message content definitely should not be visible outside the intended conversation, and identity details should be kept to what the user has chosen to share in the app.

When the buddy list is organized, what rules should determine who appears there and how contacts are grouped or labeled, especially for contacts whose visibility is limited to what the user has chosen to share?

Only people the user has added or allowed should appear in the buddy list, and blocked contacts should not show up as normal buddies. I’d expect each contact to be labeled with the presence information the user is permitted to see, like online, offline, or maybe what they’re watching if that’s available. If a contact has limited visibility, then the list should simply show the allowed subset rather than exposing anything extra.
When a contact’s block status changes, should they appear differently in the buddy list or disappear entirely, and what should happen to their presence label if the user later unblocks them?

When a contact is blocked, I’d expect them to disappear from the normal buddy list or at least be clearly separated from active contacts, not shown like a regular buddy. If the user unblocks them later, their presence label should come back normally based on whatever status is currently available, like online or offline. The key thing is that blocking should remove them from everyday use, and unblocking should restore the usual display without any special leftover state.
After delivery, who would be expected to own ongoing maintenance and support for this prototype, and are there any handoff, exception, or fallback arrangements if the intended owner can’t take it on?

I’d expect Philips Digital Systems Laboratories to own the ongoing maintenance and support, since this is their platform demonstration. If the intended owner can’t take it on, we’d need to verify an alternate support arrangement internally, but I don’t have a defined fallback path today. For the prototype, I’d assume the handoff is to the same team that will operate or demo the platform.

If Philips Digital Systems Laboratories can’t take on the support after the prototype is handed off, what internal team or process should step in, and under what conditions would that fallback arrangement be used?

I don’t have a confirmed backup team named for that yet. If Philips Digital Systems Laboratories can’t own it, we’d need a temporary internal support assignment through the project sponsor or delivery lead until an official owner is identified. That fallback would only be used if the intended handoff target is unavailable or unable to accept responsibility at the end of the prototype.

Under what conditions would the temporary internal support assignment through the project sponsor or delivery lead actually take over, and what would that team be expected to do until an official owner is identified?

It would take over only if the intended receiving team formally rejects the handoff, misses the acceptance window, or is otherwise unavailable at go-live. In that case, the temporary team would keep the prototype running, handle basic troubleshooting, and be the point of contact for defects or access issues. They wouldn’t be expected to do major enhancements, just keep things stable until ownership is formally assigned.

What operational limits should the temporary support team follow while it is covering the prototype—for example, who can authorize fixes or access changes, and are there any categories of issues or changes it should escalate rather than handle directly?

The temporary support team should only make routine, low-risk fixes that keep the prototype usable, and any access changes or configuration changes should be approved by the project sponsor or delivery lead. Anything that affects security, user privacy, sign-in behavior, or buddy list visibility should be escalated rather than handled directly. I’d also escalate any change that looks like a functional enhancement instead of a defect fix.
When the temporary support team is handling the prototype, what specific sign-in or account-related issues, if any, are within their scope to fix directly, and which ones should always be escalated?

They could probably handle simple things like a user being unable to sign in because of a known service outage or a misconfigured test account. Anything involving password resets, account recovery, authentication policy, or linking to a real external account should be escalated right away. If there’s any doubt about whether the issue affects account security or identity, I’d treat it as escalation.

For the TV users’ presence states, are there any situations where someone should be shown as something other than online, busy, or away—for example, when they’re viewing content, inactive, or not available—and if so, how should those cases be handled?

I’d keep the presence model pretty simple for this prototype, so online, busy, and away are the main user-controlled states. If someone is just viewing content or inactive, I’d expect that to be reflected as part of the app’s status display only if we can derive it cleanly, but I wouldn’t introduce a separate public presence state for those cases unless it’s clearly needed. If a user is not available because they’re signed out or blocked, then they should just show as offline or hidden from normal presence display.

When a user is actively watching TV or otherwise idle, are there any rules for whether an incoming message should interrupt what they’re doing versus wait quietly in the background, and what should happen in each case?

For this prototype, I’d expect incoming messages to always be made visible immediately, even if the user is watching TV or idle, because the point is to demonstrate notification on the television. I wouldn’t want messages to block the video or take over the screen completely, but there should be a clear on-screen alert that a message arrived. If the user is inactive, the notification can stay up until they respond or dismiss it.
Are there any business rules for the color, contrast, or font style of the on-screen notification and presence indicators so they stay legible under different TV lighting conditions or backgrounds?

Yes, they need to be highly legible on a TV screen, so we should use strong contrast and avoid thin or decorative fonts. I don’t have a fixed color standard yet, but the notification and presence indicators should remain readable against both bright and dark program content. If the team has accessibility or platform design guidelines, those should govern the final styling.

Which TV screen sizes, resolutions, or device types do we need to support for these notifications and presence indicators, and are there any platform-specific constraints that should change how they’re styled or positioned?

We’re targeting the Platform-i interactive television environment, so the main constraint is that it has to work on standard living-room TV displays rather than desktop-style screens. I don’t have a finalized list of screen sizes or exact resolutions, but the UI should be safe on lower-resolution TVs and avoid placing critical text near the edges. If the platform imposes a fixed safe area or overlay region, then the notifications and presence indicators should be designed to fit that.

When a notification or presence indicator has more text than comfortably fits within the platform’s safe area, what is the preferred behavior for handling the overflow on TV—such as truncation, wrapping, scrolling, or abbreviating—and are there any cases where that behavior should change?

For the prototype, I’d prefer truncation or short labels over scrolling, since scrolling text on TV can be hard to read and distracting. Wrapping is okay only if it still stays within the safe area and doesn’t make the notification feel too large or slow to scan. If the content is truly too long, then abbreviate the display text and let the full message be available when the user opens the message itself.
When nickname or presence information changes, should the buddy list and chat view refresh immediately, or is there an acceptable delay or event trigger for when those labels update?

They should refresh immediately when the system receives the change, so the buddy list and chat view stay in sync without the user having to do anything. I wouldn’t build in a deliberate delay for that. If the update can’t be confirmed right away because of connectivity or platform limits, then it should update as soon as the new status arrives.
